The biggest animal ever can slow its heart to 2 beats a minute. Stanford scientists measured it in 2019 with a suction cup sensor. It isn't even the strangest whale here. One offers its food to people. One may live more than 200 years. Every major whale, and the strangest true thing about each.
Daily, it eats about 16 tonnes of animals smaller than your finger. Blue whale. It feeds in every ocean except the Arctic. A 2021 Stanford study of 321 tagged whales measured it. You may have heard 4 tonnes a day. The new figure is 16. It lunges, its throat balloons, and its tongue pushes the water out through its baleen. The krill stay in. And that 2019 study suggests its heart already works near its limit. Its own heart may be what stops it growing bigger. The next one crashes hunts that aren't its business.
This whale has rescued seals from orcas. Humpback whale. It swims every major ocean. In 2009, NOAA's Robert Pitman photographed something off Antarctica. Quick ask before the photo. If strange true facts are your thing, subscribe. A humpback on its back, holding a seal on its chest, out of the water. You'd think humpbacks only defend their own calves. In Pitman's 2016 study of 115 encounters, 89 percent involved orcas hunting other species. Orcas get loud when they attack. Humpbacks may hear it from over a kilometer away and charge in, bellowing. It shows up first and finds out who it's saving later. The next one is the hunter. And sometimes, it shares.
It has offered its food to humans at least 34 times. Orca. It lives in every ocean on Earth. A 2025 study led by Jared Towers of Bay Cetology confirmed them across about 20 years. It swims up, drops a fish, a bird or a ray in front of you. Then it waits to see what you do. Some offer it again. You may have heard it's a whale. It's the biggest member of the dolphin family. The ocean's top predator keeps trying to share its lunch. The next one turned up in the wrong ocean.
It left the Atlantic by the 1700s. In 2024, one came back. Gray whale. It lives along the coasts of the North Pacific. In March 2024, a New England Aquarium plane spotted it off Nantucket. How? The Northwest Passage above Canada has recently been ice free in summer. That may open a route from the Pacific. You'd think it must be lost. But in 2015, Oregon State tracked one swimming 22,511 kilometers in 172 days. A whale the Atlantic lost is turning up again. The next one doesn't sing. It speaks in code.
Can a whale have an alphabet? Scientists have proposed this one does. Sperm whale. It dives around 600 meters, holding its breath up to 45 minutes. In 2024, an MIT team analyzed nearly 9,000 of its click patterns, called codas, from Dominica. Each coda is a burst of clicks with a rhythm and a tempo. You'd think each coda is fixed, like a word. Whales stretch the timing or add an extra click, depending on the exchange. Not just clicks. Clicks built from parts. The next one's famous feature isn't what you think.

5 whales down. Still ahead, a whale that may live more than 200 years. Its tusk twists 2 ways at once, and that keeps it straight. Narwhal. It lives in the high Arctic. The tusk is a tooth, up to 3 meters, taller than you. In 2026, an Aarhus University team X-rayed tusks to find out. The inner layer spirals one way, the outer layer the other. The twists cancel out, so it grows straight, like a screw. You may have heard it mainly senses the water. That team doubts it, since females rarely grow one. It's still debated. Two opposite twists make one straight tooth. Its closest relative is next. Watch its forehead.
You make faces. This whale makes them with its forehead. Beluga. It lives in Arctic and subarctic seas. In 2024, the University of Rhode Island logged 2,570 forehead shapes from 4 belugas at Mystic Aquarium. That bump is the melon, a pad of soft fat. Belugas push it, press it, lift it, or shake it like jelly. You'd think the melon only aims sound. But almost every shape came during social moments, mostly from males. You make faces with muscle. It makes them with fat. The next one's voice reaches below the seafloor.
Scientists used its song to see inside the seafloor. Fin whale. It cruises deep water in every major ocean. In 2021, Oregon State caught its calls on 54 seafloor sensors. The calls sit near the bottom of your hearing, and they're as loud as big ships. Part of each call echoed back up through the rock. Timing those echoes mapped layers over 2 kilometers deep. You'd think that takes ships firing air guns. This time, a whale did it. Its song doubles as a seafloor scanner. The next one wears its ID on its face.
Those white patches on its head are crawling with whale lice. North Atlantic right whale. It lives off the east coast of North America. The patches are rough skin, turned white by tiny crustaceans. Each pattern is different, so scientists can identify and count them. The Right Whale Consortium's latest estimate, released in 2025, is 384. You'd think the name is a compliment. Whalers are said to have called it the right whale to hunt. It floated after death. Fewer than 400 left, each known by its face. The last one is its Arctic cousin. Hunters found something old inside one.
Inside one, hunters found a harpoon tip from the 1800s. Bowhead whale. It lives among Arctic sea ice. That whale was caught off Alaska in 2007, and experts dated the tip to 1885 to 1895. It had carried it for over a century. Scientists later read a chemical clock in bowhead eyes. One came out at about 211 years, nearly 3 human lifetimes. A 2025 study in Nature found a clue. Its cells make far more of a protein that repairs broken DNA. You'd think a giant this old would get cancer often. Its cells gather fewer cancer mutations. It doesn't avoid damage. It fixes it.
Its heart may limit the biggest whale. Its cells may keep the oldest alive. Which surprised you most? The orca offering food, or the bowhead that may live 200 years? Next, every type of shark. One may outlive the bowhead. Thanks for watching.
